text.p: Japan took "half-a-step" forward in its assessment of the economy, but the recovery continues to give mixed signals as the effects of a sales tax rise in April still sit heavily on its shoulders.

"Compared to last month, our assessment has become 'half a step' or 'two-thirds of a step' stronger," Economic Planning Agency (EPA) Minister Taro Aso said on Friday after the release of the government's latest monthly economic report.
But the wording of the report, closely watched for clues to the government's economic policy, painted a more mixed picture.
"Although the tempo of the recovery has temporarily slowed down, the economy is continuing to recover, centering around firm private demand," the report said.
Until last month, the ministry maintained a view that Japan's economy was continuing to improve and private demand was firm, although the pace of the recovery was gradual.
Japan's economy has been in a slow recovery since late 1993 after the collapse of the "bubble" economy of inflated stock and land prices in late 1980s.
However, the Japanese government has not been convinced that the economy is back on an expansion track.
In explaining the change of the wording, the first since November 1996, an EPA official said the word "gradual" was dropped in describing the basic trend of recovery.
"The 'undercurrent' of the economy could no longer be described as 'gradual' as the recovery was now centering around private demand," he said.
But the official added that in contrast, the recovery was still being hit by the negative effects of a tax rise in April and remained 'gradual'.
A fall in private consumption was the most notable effect of the rise in the national sales tax to five percent from three percent on April 1, he said.

Despite a rising trend in production and an improvement in employment conditions which were supporting the recovery, he said the ministry was still in the process of judging the effects of the tax rise.
"It's still too early to become optimistic or pessimistic over the outcome of the tax rise," he said.
Although minister Aso said the economy had almost gotten over the negative impact of the tax measure by June, he said it was too soon to consider an increase in the current record-low interest rates.
The Bank of Japan has kept the official discount rate, which it charges on loans to commercial banks, at a low of 0.5 percent since September 1995 to help boost the economy.
There has been speculation in the financial markets that the central bank may raise rates when it is assured that the economy is on a self-sustaining recovery.

Financial markets reacted little to the change in the government's assessment of the economy, but some currency operators said the report clearly suggested a more positive assessement of the economy by the government.
